channel.title: Daily Recap — 🚀 Space News
channel.description: What happened in 🚀 Space News, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine draw a funding threat from Congress
item.description:
SpaceX's military satellite service Starshield is under scrutiny after changes made to the service in Ukraine in October 2026, and the incoming chair of the House committee overseeing it is now threatening SpaceX's funding. The dispute centers on what exactly changed and why — questions SpaceX is being pressed to answer in writing.

The stakes go beyond one contract: Starshield is the backbone of SpaceX's growing military business, and a funding fight in Congress could ripple into its broader Pentagon work. It's also the latest sign that SpaceX's dual role — commercial spaceflight giant and defense contractor entangled in an active war — keeps pulling it into political fights it can't easily fly above.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

item.title: SpaceX's lenders don't want their collateral launched into orbit
item.description:
SpaceX's bondholders want the company's valuable chip collateral kept on Earth and within reach — not launched into space, where it would be rather hard to repossess. The dispute highlights the strange new world of space finance: when your collateral is destined for orbit, traditional lending protections start to break down.

It's a real constraint on SpaceX's ambitions for space-based data centers. Lenders are happy to fund hardware they can seize if things go wrong; hardware circling the planet at 17,000 mph is a different proposition. How this gets resolved could set the template for financing the entire space data center industry.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space

item.title: NASA's new Moon plan is taking shape, but big questions remain
item.description:
NASA's revised plan for returning astronauts to the Moon is coming into focus, but key technical and programmatic questions are still being debated. The agency is working through architecture choices that will determine how — and how soon — crews get back to the lunar surface.

The debate matters because the Moon program has already been reshaped multiple times, and each revision carries schedule and cost consequences. For now, the plan exists in outline with the details still contested, which is a familiar place for Artemis-era planning — but the clock is ticking, and the longer the big questions stay open, the harder the timeline gets.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain

item.title: Rocket Report: a weekend of ups and downs, and Stoke hits an engine milestone
item.description:
This week's Rocket Report rounds up a mixed weekend in launch news, including Russia launching a Soyuz rocket carrying satellites intended to help enable drone attacks over Ukraine — a reminder that orbital launches remain entangled with the war. On the brighter side, Stoke Space celebrated a milestone for its engine program as it pushes toward a fully reusable rocket.

The weekly roundup remains the best single digest of an industry where the launch cadence keeps climbing and the line between commercial spaceflight and geopolitics keeps blurring. Stoke's progress is worth watching: a working reusable second stage would be a genuine step change, not just another incremental improvement.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone

item.title: Curiosity photographs drifting twilight clouds and notches 49 drill samples
item.description:
NASA's Curiosity rover caught drifting twilight clouds over Gale Crater on October 31, its 5,061st Martian day. The rover uses its navigation cameras to capture the post-sunset clouds, which appear for only a short time each fall — a brief, beautiful window into Martian weather.

Meanwhile, a new collage shows all 49 drill holes Curiosity has made as of November 2026, each one a rock sample pulverized and analyzed by instruments inside the rover. Fourteen years into a mission planned for two, Curiosity is still doing real science: every sample adds to the picture of whether Mars was once habitable, and the clouds add a seasonal rhythm to a world that often looks frozen in time.

Sources

  • NASA: Curiosity Spots Drifting Twilight Clouds
  • NASA: NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover Collects Samples

item.title: NASA seeds 302 small-business projects with up to $171 million
item.description:
NASA's Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer programs have selected 302 projects for seed funding, totaling up to $171 million. The awards go to small businesses around the country working on technologies NASA needs for Moon and Mars exploration.

It's one of those quiet programs that punches above its weight: small firms get the capital to develop ideas that might otherwise die in a lab, and NASA gets a pipeline of technology it couldn't build in-house. The space economy angle matters too — the funding is explicitly meant to fuel US commercial space capability, not just NASA's own missions.

Sources

  • NASA: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation

item.title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth
item.description:
Voyager 1, humanity's farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth — about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) — after more than 49 years of constant travel. The probe crossed the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) on November 18.

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, and Voyager 1 is now the first human-made object to get that far from home. The milestone is a reminder of just how durable the 1977-era spacecraft has proven to be: it is still returning data from interstellar space nearly half a century after launch, operating on instruments and power systems designed long before most of today's spaceflight era began.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA's Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth

item.title: Google turns to Blue Origin for its space-based solar project
item.description:
Google is turning to Blue Origin for launch services for Project Suncatcher, its long-term moonshot to put solar power generation in space. The project envisions satellites collecting solar energy in orbit, where sunlight is uninterrupted, though it remains a far-future concept rather than a near-term product.

The deal is notable as a sign of Blue Origin's growing role as a launch provider for major tech customers, but Google's bigger challenge isn't the rocket — it's the underlying economics and engineering of beaming power from orbit at scale. Suncatcher remains an early-stage bet, and the launch partnership is one small step on a very long road.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains

item.title: NASA's new Moon plans create a problem for Orion
item.description:
NASA's revised approach to lunar landings is putting new demands on the Orion spacecraft, which was not originally designed to fly the profile the updated plans require. The changes are meant to make Moon landings easier overall, but they shift complexity onto Orion and its crew systems.

Agency officials are cautioning against moving too fast or cutting corners to meet the new architecture, emphasizing a responsibility to keep the program safe even as schedules tighten. The tension captures the central trade-off of the current Artemis reshaping: simplifying one part of the mission tends to complicate another, and Orion — the one piece that must carry astronauts home — is absorbing much of that burden.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way

item.title: NASA test-fires RS-25 engine for future Artemis missions
item.description:
NASA fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 on November 18 at the Fred Haise Test Stand at Stennis Space Center in Mississippi, running the developmental engine for its planned full duration of 200 seconds. The test supports future Artemis missions that will rely on the RS-25, the Space Launch System's main engine.

The engine tested is a developmental unit that will not itself fly, but the hot-fire data feeds directly into the flight engines that will power upcoming Artemis launches. Steady progress on engine testing is one of the quieter but essential threads of the Artemis program: every successful long-duration firing de-risks the crewed missions that depend on the SLS stack performing exactly as designed.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Conducts Latest RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions

item.title: NASA data powers a way to find pulsars a million times faster
item.description:
Open data from NASA's Fermi mission helped an international team of scientists develop a method for finding pulsars about a million times faster than before. Pulsars — rapidly spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radiation across space — are valuable tools for studying extreme physics and testing general relativity, but the faint or unusual ones have been painstakingly hard to spot.

The breakthrough matters beyond a single catalog: faster pulsar discovery accelerates the search for gravitational-wave sources and deepens our map of the Milky Way's most extreme objects. It's also a win for open science — the result came not from a new telescope, but from researchers finding a smarter way to mine data NASA had already made freely available.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars

item.title: Voyager 1 passes one light-day from Earth, a first for any human-made object
item.description:
NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft passed one light-day away from Earth on November 17, 2026 — a distance no other human-made object has ever reached. To mark the milestone, the Empire State Building was illuminated in gold, a nod to the gold-plated copper phonograph record aboard the spacecraft: the Golden Record, carrying sounds and images of Earth into interstellar space.

Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 has now been traveling for nearly half a century, and historians revisiting the Golden Record's creation say they are confident the record will last a very long time. The one-light-day mark is a reminder of just how far humanity's farthest emissary has gone — and how durable the message it carries may prove to be.

Sources

  • NASA: Empire State Building Goes Gold for Voyager
  • Space - Ars Technica: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details

item.title: ULA blames Vulcan failure on inadequate fuel supply to engines
item.description:
United Launch Alliance says the failure of its Vulcan rocket was caused by an inadequate fuel supply to the engines. The company has not yet detailed the full corrective plan, but the finding narrows the investigation to the propellant feed system rather than the engines themselves.

Vulcan is a linchpin of ULA's future — and of the US Space Force's launch plans — so the path back to flight matters well beyond one rocket. ULA remains, in NASA's words, a valued partner, and the focus now shifts to how quickly the fuel-supply issue can be fixed and the vehicle cleared to fly again.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says

item.title: NASA data clinches the first confirmed stellar merger of its kind
item.description:
Researchers have identified a first of its kind: a star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. The newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star has been nicknamed Bao, and the NASA-funded discovery was bolstered by quick-turn observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Stellar mergers have long been predicted but never before confirmed in this form, making Bao a landmark case for understanding how stars live, collide, and are reborn. The discovery also shows off Webb's ability to pivot fast to follow up on a tantalizing find — a capability that is becoming central to modern astronomy.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger

item.title: NASA sets November 29 for the next space station cargo launch
item.description:
NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST on Sunday, November 29, for the next cargo launch to the International Space Station. The Northrop Grumman Cygnus spacecraft will carry approximately 11,000 pounds of science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the orbiting laboratory, with a prelaunch media teleconference set for Monday, November 23.

The mission, CRS-25, keeps the station's steady resupply cadence going as the ISS continues its science program. Coverage plans are now set, and barring weather or technical delays, the launch will close out November with another delivery run to low Earth orbit.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Sets Coverage for Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Launch, Prelaunch

item.title: NASA challenges US companies to build better electric rocket engines
item.description:
NASA has launched a new competition inviting US companies to build prototypes of mid-power Hall effect thrusters, a type of electric propulsion considered crucial for future space operations and exploration. Hall effect thrusters use an electric field to accelerate a propellant gas, producing efficient thrust for long-duration missions — the kind of steady, fuel-sipping push needed to move satellites and deep-space spacecraft.

The challenge is aimed at maturing a technology that sits between today's small satellite thrusters and the high-power systems future missions will need. For the companies competing, it is a chance to prove hardware that could end up powering everything from satellite constellations to crewed exploration.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Announces Mid-Power Electric Rocket Challenge for US Companies

item.title: NASA's NICER telescope ends science operations after eight years
item.description:
NASA's NICER telescope aboard the International Space Station has ended science operations after eight years in orbit, including six and a half years beyond its original mission plan. The Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer spent its career timing the X-ray pulses of neutron stars with extraordinary precision, using those measurements to probe the physics of matter crushed to densities far beyond anything reproducible on Earth.

The mission's legacy is a set of the tightest constraints yet on the size and structure of neutron stars, plus a successful demonstration of pulsar-based navigation that could one day let deep-space spacecraft find their way without ground contact. NASA and station teams are now winding down the instrument and finalizing plans for its end-of-mission disposition.

Sources

  • NASA: NICER Status Updates

item.title: Vulcan failure may not be a BE-4 engine problem, early evidence suggests
item.description:
The investigation into ULA's Vulcan rocket failure is shaping up to be a complex one, and preliminary data suggests the BE-4 engines built by Blue Origin may not be to blame. That's a significant early signal, since the engines were an obvious suspect for a new rocket whose first flights had gone smoothly, and it shifts attention toward other systems on the vehicle.

Details remain closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, so this is far from a conclusion — early failure data is often revised as engineers dig into telemetry. But if the engines are cleared, the fix could be narrower and faster than a propulsion redesign, which matters for Vulcan's role in national security launches and its competition with SpaceX for high-value missions.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines

item.title: SpaceX Dragon set to depart the space station with research samples
item.description:
A SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft is scheduled to undock from the International Space Station no earlier than Wednesday, November 18, wrapping up the 35th commercial resupply mission. Weather permitting, it will depart the Harmony module's space-facing port at 11:05 a.m. EST, carrying scientific research samples and hardware back to Earth for NASA and its international partners.

The returning cargo is the real prize: experiments conducted in microgravity lose value if their samples degrade, so a prompt splashdown and recovery keeps months of station science intact. NASA will provide live coverage of the departure.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure

item.title: NASA's Space Apps Challenge breaks records with 182,000 participants
item.description:
NASA's annual Space Apps Challenge drew a record 181,835 registered participants across 593 events worldwide over the weekend of November 14-15. The hackathon invites teams to tackle one of 14 challenges using NASA's open data, spanning space exploration and Earth science problems.

The scale is the story here: what began as a modest outreach event has become one of the largest hackathons on the planet, with participation up sharply from prior years. For NASA, it's a pipeline — the event turns its open datasets into working prototypes and introduces a huge, global audience to space science, some of whom will go on to careers in the field.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records

item.title: Chandra turns baby stars into sound in a new album of sonifications
item.description:
NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory has released a new album of sonifications — data from actively forming stars, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes, translated into sound. The four new pieces let listeners hear the structure of stellar nurseries across the galaxy and beyond, with different pitches and tones mapping to features in the X-ray and optical data.

Sonification is more than a novelty: it gives researchers another way to perceive patterns in complex datasets, and it makes the science accessible to people who experience the universe better through hearing than sight. The new tracks join Chandra's growing catalog of cosmic sounds, which has become one of NASA's most popular public outreach formats.

Sources

  • NASA: New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA's Chandra

item.title: Another satellite firm wants its own rocket — and this one has a real case
item.description:
Yet another satellite company is angling for dedicated launch capacity, but this bid stands apart from the usual hype: the argument is sovereignty, not scale. As one executive put it, governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most — a recognition that relying on foreign launch providers leaves European satellite networks exposed to someone else's schedule, pricing, and politics.

The context is a launch market still dominated by SpaceX, where smaller operators struggle to get rides on their own terms. A satellite company with its own rocket, or at least a guaranteed path to orbit, can promise customers continuity that a rideshare slot can't. Whether the economics work is the open question, but the strategic logic — especially in Europe — is hard to dismiss.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Yet another satellite company is jockeying for a rocket—but this one makes sense

item.title: Perseverance finds ghostly rocks that may hold signs of ancient Martian water — and maybe life
item.description:
While investigating "Idubi," an area of ancient Martian crust in the Lac de Charmes region outside Jezero crater, NASA's Perseverance rover found a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks standing out sharply against the darker, dust-covered surface. Data from the SuperCam instrument has now confirmed these rocks are not igneous in origin, as the team first suspected, but are rich in hydrated silica.

Hydrated silica forms in aqueous environments on Earth, including hydrothermal, groundwater, and soil systems, several of which could have supported life. It also has a remarkable capacity to preserve microfossils, making these deposits prime astrobiology targets. Perseverance had found silica-rich rocks before on Jezero's inner rim, but they were too small for detailed study. The Idubi rocks are on a much more promising scale, and a detailed proximity science campaign is already underway to look for signs of ancient life.

Sources

  • NASA: Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago

item.title: When will humans actually fly on Starship? Not soon — and maybe not from Earth first
item.description:
Ars Technica's analysis of the Starship human spaceflight timeline comes with a warning up front: all estimates should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt. If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight, it could happen reasonably quickly — but the answer depends on what "human spaceflight" means. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from Earth or land here. They will likely be NASA's lunar astronauts, who launch aboard Orion and transfer to Starship for the trip to the Moon's surface.

History counsels skepticism: the original target for launching humans on Starship, then called the Interplanetary Transport System, was 2024. NASA's Starship lunar landing has slipped from 2024 to 2028, and SpaceX has reportedly told prospective customers that commercial flights could begin in 2029, a date the article treats as unconfirmed. The author's assessment: don't expect humans to land on Earth in Starship before 2030, plausibly not until the mid-2030s. Flight 15, which launched November 13, proved the Ship can return from orbit and be caught, but left orbital propellant transfer, a crew cabin, and certification undemonstrated.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: When will humans actually fly on Starship?

item.title: The last ice on Puncak Jaya
item.description:
Ice near the summit of Puncak Jaya, in Indonesia's Sudirman Range on the island of New Guinea, has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers. The range is one of the few places near the equator that has long held ice year-round, and scientists have described its glaciers as high-altitude "canaries in the coal mine" for a warming climate.

The scale of the loss is stark. In 1988 the glaciers covered about 4.31 square kilometers; by September 2025 only about 0.09 square kilometers remained, roughly 2 percent of the 1988 extent. The ice has also thinned dramatically, from 32 meters thick at the main monitoring site in 2010 to 4 meters in 2023, and by November 2024 the ice there was gone entirely. As glaciers thin they break apart, exposing more edges to melt — a "house of cards problem," in one glaciologist's words. Small remnants persist in high crevices, but their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over, and the main ice could disappear entirely around 2030, possibly sooner with the current El Niño.

Sources

  • NASA: The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya

item.title: NASA earns its 16th straight clean financial audit
item.description:
For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or "clean," opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements. It is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that the agency's financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present NASA's financial position.

Sixteen straight clean audits is a long run of financial discipline for an agency that manages one of the largest and most complex budgets in the federal government, spanning human spaceflight, science missions, and aeronautics. The streak matters as a signal of institutional health: whatever the debates about NASA's programs and priorities, its books have passed independent scrutiny every year since 2011.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion

item.title: Webb captures a star-forming region in all its chaos
item.description:
Today's Astronomy Picture of the Day features the James Webb Space Telescope's infrared view of NGC 7129, a star-forming region where gravity pulls massive amounts of gas together while previously formed stars complicate the picture with powerful jets and winds. Opaque dust can block visible-light images, but Webb's infrared vision cuts through it to reveal stars at different stages of development.

In the image, the young stars on the left, embedded in gold-colored gas, are typically more mature than those on the right, in the red region, where jets and winds likely cause the gas's filamentary shape. Studying stars at different stages in a single region helps astronomers work out which physical processes matter most, and when, in the messy business of star formation.

Sources

  • NASA: APOD: 2026 November 16 – NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb

item.title: Curiosity's drill holes, all 49 of them
item.description:
NASA has published a collage of all 49 drill holes made by the Curiosity rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity's drill, mounted on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock into instruments in the rover's belly that analyze its composition.

It is a quiet milestone worth pausing on: 49 holes drilled into another planet, each one a small act of field geology performed by a robot that has been roving Mars since 2012. Taken together, the samples form a record of the planet's changing chemistry and climate, and they remain the ground truth against which orbital observations and newer missions like Perseverance are measured.

Sources

  • NASA: A Collage Showing 49 Drill Holes Made by NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover

item.title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, a major blow to SpaceX's competitors
item.description:
United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket failed during launch, destroying its payload — the first total mission failure in ULA's 20-year history. The rocket was carrying Amazon Leo satellites, and the loss is a major blow to SpaceX's competitors: Amazon's Leo constellation is already well behind Starlink, and losing a full launch load sets its deployment schedule back further.

Vulcan is also a key vehicle for US national security launches, so the failure will draw scrutiny beyond Amazon's program. An investigation will determine what went wrong, but the immediate picture is stark — two decades of reliability ended in a single launch, and the race to challenge Starlink just got harder.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
